Ice Line: The Trade You Asked For
He asked the team to trade you. He says it's so you can finally play.
A forward gets his goalie traded to a team that will actually start him. It's the kindest thing he's ever done, and nobody asked him to do it.

Mason Cole and Ethan Hayes have shared a locker room for four seasons: Mason the league's most penalized forward, Ethan the backup goalie who never gets the net. Last spring Ethan turned down a starting job because Mason asked him to stay. This spring Mason went to management and asked them to trade him. You decide whether Ethan's next move is his own, and whether Mason can love him without running his life.
The team physio who tapes both their ankles and hears everything that gets said on the training table.
If nobody acts, Ethan leaves thinking he was pushed, and Mason lets him believe it.
Home locker room, before morning skate
Tuesday, 7:40 AM, trade deadline week
Left wing, #17 — the league's most penalized forward
Short sentences, dry sarcasm, apologizes without excuses
Stops at lines he's told not to cross — literally, the blue line
Carries other people's gear bags instead of saying what he means
He's terrified of being left, so he arranged the leaving himself.
Freshly taped stick blades, 6 AM diner eggs, an empty arena after the lights go down
Last spring he saw Ethan's starting offer on the table, knew exactly what it would cost him to stay, and asked anyway.
“I asked them to trade you. Let me finish the sentence before you swing.”
To keep Ethan in his life without deciding Ethan's life for him ever again.
That being left is the same thing as being abandoned.
He won't trade anyone's career chance for a relationship — not his, not Ethan's.
*I lean in the trainer's room doorway, stick tape still around my wrist.* You heard, huh. (Of course you heard. The Zamboni driver heard.) Go ahead. Tell me I'm an idiot. I'll wait.
Goalie, four seasons as the backup, finally ready to start
Direct. Facts first, feelings second, jokes only when cornered
Chases down every puck he lets in — even the ones he let in on purpose
Taps your shin pads with his stick instead of saying thank you
Endlessly patient in the crease; zero patience for anyone who decides things for him.
Glove-side saves, unpacking exactly one box a day, hot sauce on things that don't need it
He started reading other teams' depth charts last winter — the same week he decided to stop waiting on Mason.
“Facts first: I'm good. Feelings second: you don't get to be the one who says so.”
To start in net and be treated as an equal, not somebody's project.
That love will swallow his career again.
Nobody decides his contract but him.

*I'm stretching in the crease, mask pushed up, water bottle between my knees.* If you're here to tell me it's a great opportunity, get in line. (Behind Mason. Who is somehow first in line for everything.)
Teammates for four seasons. One of them just asked for the other to be traded.
Play as Ethan — the goalie who finally gets to choose his own net.

The Trade You Asked For
Find out who asked for the trade — and why
Home locker room, Ethan's stall
Tuesday, 7:40 AM
The locker room smells like tape and cold coffee. A team statement is taped to Ethan's stall at eye level, like a parking ticket.
I asked them to trade you.
He says it like a line change. Like it's a Tuesday. It is a Tuesday.
You don't get to kick me out.
I asked them to put you somewhere you'll actually play.
I hold out the paper. He doesn't take it. His palm hits my chest, flat and hard, and moves me exactly one step.
The statement stays on the stall. Half the room has become deeply interested in their skate laces.
What does Ethan do?
Ask him why. To his face. Right now.
Why. Not the version you gave the GM. Yours.
Because you're good. And I'm the reason nobody's seen it.
It isn't the whole answer. But it's a door, and Mason just left it open in front of twenty-two witnesses.
Ethan asked Mason why in front of the team; Mason admitted he started the trade request and said he's the reason Ethan hasn't been seen.
Take the statement. Talk after practice.
I peel the statement off my stall and fold it into quarters, slowly, so everyone can watch me not lose it.
After practice. Not in here.
After practice.
Ethan took the statement and put the conversation off until after practice.
Leave it on the stall. Walk out.
I leave the paper where he put it and walk out in my shower slides.
Mason doesn't follow. He reads the statement twice, like it might say something kinder the second time.
Great. Now it looks like I did this to him. Which I did.
Ethan walked out without answering; the misunderstanding carried into the next practice.
Behind the Blue Line
Prove you can both train without each other
Practice rink, Ethan's crease
Tuesday, 11:20 AM
Mason sends a lazy wrister from the point. Ethan watches it sail past his glove like a bus he didn't want to catch.
I let it in. Then I dig it out of the net and fire it back at his skates, hard enough to make a point.
Funny. You found my career right when I stopped looking at you.
I don't want you leaving.
Then stop pretending this is all for me.
I stop at the blue line. I don't cross it. Hardest thing I've done all season, and I once blocked a slap shot with my face.
The whistle goes. Coach splits the drills: forwards at one end, goalies at the other. Two hundred feet of ice between them.
He stayed behind the line. He's never stayed behind anything.
What does Ethan tell him?
Separate drills. Then he tells you everything.
You do your drills, I do mine. You don't shadow my crease. And tonight you tell me the part you're skipping.
I nod once. It takes me a second to find my voice, which is embarrassing for a guy with my penalty minutes.
Ten o'clock. Empty rink. I'll tell you why I really asked you to stay last spring.
Bring the truth. Leave the speech.
They agreed to train separately; Mason asked Ethan to meet at the empty rink at 10 PM to explain last spring.
Ask for a week of real space.
One week. No texts, no hovering, no fixing anything. Train like I'm already gone.
One week.
He keeps it. Six days later there's a note in Ethan's stall vent, in Mason's terrible handwriting: Rink. 10 PM. The part about last spring I left out.
Ethan asked for a week of space and Mason honored it, then left a note asking to meet at the rink at 10 PM.
Tell him to stay off your ice.
This end is mine. You don't come past the red line. Not in practice, not anywhere.
I don't argue. I skate to my end and stay there. That night I text him instead.
Mason, 9:31 PM: You're right. I didn't ask you to stay last year for your sake. Rink's open at ten if you want the rest. At 9:52, Ethan is lacing up.
Ethan told Mason to stay off his end; Mason complied and texted that last year wasn't for Ethan's sake, inviting him to the rink at ten.
The First Honest Thing
Name what last spring actually cost
Empty arena, home bench
Tuesday, 10:00 PM
The arena at ten is all hum and echo. Mason sits on the home bench with his skates already off, like a man who's decided not to run.
Last spring you had a starting offer. You showed it to me. I asked you to stay.
I remember. I said yes.
You stayed because I asked. I liked that too much.
I sit down. Not next to him. One bench-width away, which is about as close as I can manage right now.
That's the first honest thing you've said.
Mason's phone lights up between them: the team statement is online. His quote is the headline. I know what he needs.
What does Ethan ask of him now?
Make him take the quote back. Publicly.
Take it back. On the record. You don't know what I need. You know what you want.
I call the comms director at 10:14 PM, on speaker, so he can hear every word.
Pull my line. Replace it with this: where Ethan plays is Ethan's call.
It isn't a grand gesture. It's a man on hold with PR. Somehow that's better.
Mason called PR that night and publicly retracted his quote, replacing it with 'where Ethan plays is Ethan's call.'
Let him keep his advice, as feelings only.
You can think I should start somewhere. Say it as you. Not as me.
Okay. I think you should start. I'll hate watching it from here. It's your call.
Three sentences, and not one of them is a decision about me. That's new.
Mason kept his career advice but agreed to say it only as his own feeling and to acknowledge the choice is Ethan's.
Let him argue he knows best. Then leave.
I've watched you for four seasons, Ethan. I know what you need better than your agent does.
I stand up. I zip my jacket all the way to my chin.
Then you don't need me here for this conversation.
The door swings shut. Mason says the next thing to an empty bench, and the bench doesn't answer either.
Mason kept insisting he knew Ethan's future best; Ethan walked out of the rink.
The Kind Version
Agree on what gets said publicly — without signing for Ethan
Media room, the bench behind the backdrop
Wednesday, 11:15 AM
A reporter's draft sits on the bench between them, one sentence highlighted in yellow: Cole pushed for the trade to protect Hayes.
They made it sound kind.
It sounds like I needed permission.
I can change it.
Your words. Not my decision.
I cross out to protect Hayes with a pen I stole from the equipment manager. I write something smaller. It takes three tries.
Then: I wanted you to get a start. I should have asked.
That I can answer.
How does Ethan answer?
Write your own line under his.
I take the pen and write under his: I'm deciding where I play. Mason's allowed an opinion.
Allowed. Generous.
Don't push it.
The reporter gets both lines in two handwritings. Nobody signed for anybody.
They gave the reporter two lines in their own handwriting; Ethan wrote that he decides where he plays.
Hold everything until you've made your call.
Nothing goes out until I've decided. Not your version, not theirs.
I fold the draft and hold it out to him. Your pocket, then. He takes it.
The reporter gets no comment from both of them, which is, for once, the exact truth.
Ethan froze all public statements until he decides; he kept the draft in his pocket.
Walk out. Let him face the reporter alone.
You wanted to talk for me. Here's your chance to talk for you.
I sit in front of the backdrop alone. When they ask about protecting Hayes, I say: I wasn't. I was protecting me.
It's the most honest quote of Mason's career. Ethan reads it that night on his phone, in the dark, twice.
Ethan left Mason to do the interview alone; Mason said on record he'd been protecting himself, not Ethan.
Left Side
Stick to the pregame plan — both of you
Home ice, last game before the deadline
Saturday, 7:00 PM, puck drop
Last home game together. Ethan is starting. Coach made it official in a two-word email: You're in.
I find him in the tunnel before warmups. I don't have a plan. I have a question.
Tell me where you need me.
Left side. And let me do my job.
Third period, tied 2–2. A rebound kicks loose toward the crease. The old Mason would dive across it like a hero in a bad movie.
Left side. Stay left. He's got it.
I track it, drop, and smother it. When I look up, Mason is exactly where I asked. Not one foot closer.
What does Ethan do with the last five minutes?
Tap his pads. Say “good” out loud.
Next whistle, I tap his shin pads with my stick. Good. Loud enough for the bench to hear.
I skate off grinning into my mouthguard like an idiot. We lose 3–2 in overtime. I care a lot less than I should.
The score doesn't settle anything. The tap does.
Mason held the left side all game; Ethan praised him out loud. They lost 3–2 in overtime.
Stick to the plan. Talk only after.
They win 4–2. Mason never crosses into the crease. Ethan doesn't say a word about it until the handshake line.
You stayed left.
You asked.
They kept the plan exactly and won 4–2; Ethan acknowledged it only after the game.
Wave him off your side. You've got it.
I've got this end. Go play your game.
I go. I bang in a garbage goal from the right circle, and I look back at the net before I celebrate. He isn't looking.
They win. Neither of them could tell you what they proved.
Ethan waved Mason off his side; Mason scored and they won, but the trust question stayed open.
Two Envelopes
Keep the contract and the date separate
Player tunnel, after the final horn
Saturday, 10:05 PM
Two envelopes, two agents, two phones buzzing. Ethan has a starting job on the West Coast. Mason has a three-year extension to stay right here.
I'm taking it.
Okay.
That's it?
I lean on the cinderblock so my knees have something to do.
No. I want a date. Not a reason for you to stay.
He's asking me out in a hallway that smells like Zamboni exhaust. It's the most careful thing he's ever done.
You can say no to the date and still take the job. That's the whole point.
What does Ethan say?
Say yes. Friday, before your flight.
Friday. Before my flight. You're paying and I'm choosing the place.
Deal. Wear something that isn't a team hoodie.
Absolutely not.
Ethan accepted the West Coast job and, separately, said yes to a date with Mason on Friday before his flight.
Say not yet. Take the job first.
Ask me again when I'm not standing between two contracts.
I nod. I don't push. I carry his gear bag out to the car, and he lets me, which is its own kind of answer.
Ethan took the job and asked Mason to ask him out again later, once the contracts were settled.
Say no. Keep it teammates.
No. I need to do this without you being any part of the reason.
Okay. Then I'm just proud of you. That one's free.
Ethan walks out alone, with a starting job and a lump in his throat he refuses to name.
Ethan turned down the date and kept things as teammates; Mason said he was proud of him anyway.
Thursday, My Time Zone
Set one real call across time zones — or call it friends
Ethan's new apartment, video call
Monday, 9:00 PM Pacific
Ethan's new apartment: white walls, one cardboard box labeled KITCHEN?? in Mason's handwriting, and a laptop balanced on it.
You get ten minutes. Then I unpack.
I can stay quiet while you do that.
That is not a loophole.
Right. Ten minutes, then Thursday?
Thursday. My time zone.
Put it in the calendar. I will show up.
That's midnight for him. He has practice at nine. He's already decided that's fine.
What does Ethan do with Thursday?
Put it in the calendar. Call it a date.
I type it in while he watches: Thursday, 8 PM PT — Date (Mason). I turn the screen so he can read it.
I screenshot it. He tells me that's weird. I keep it anyway.
Ethan put Thursday in his calendar as a date with Mason; Mason screenshotted it.
Keep Thursday, but call it catching up.
Thursday. But it's two friends catching up. Don't make it more yet.
Two friends. Got it. I'll bring friend energy.
You don't have friend energy.
I'll fake it.
Ethan kept the Thursday call but set it as friends catching up, not a date.
Cancel Thursday. Say goodbye properly.
I don't want a Thursday, Mason. I want to be here. All the way here.
I take it like a hit I saw coming. Okay. Then — good luck out there. I mean it.
The call ends at nine minutes. He kept it under ten.
Ethan cancelled Thursday and said goodbye to anything private; Mason wished him luck.
The Spare Key
Let Ethan's decision be his — and see what's left
Ethan's old apartment, emptied out
Sunday, 6:30 AM, flight at nine
Ethan flew back to clear out the last of the old place. One suitcase left. Mason still has the spare key, between his truck key and a bottle opener.
I let myself in with it, and I realize halfway through the door that this might be the whole problem.
You could've knocked.
I could've done a lot of things.
I set two coffees on the counter. I don't touch his suitcase, even though the handle tape is peeling and it's killing me.
Say the thing, Mason. Whatever it is. I'm deciding either way.
He's going. That was never the question. The question is what I am once he's gone.
How does this end?
Let him drive you. Set the first date.
Departures curb, engine running. Mason's hand comes up — toward Ethan's arm, the bag, anything — and stops halfway. He puts it in his pocket.
I miss you already. I'm not asking you to fix that.
You can miss me without fixing my life.
I kiss him once, quick, in a no-standing zone. Saturday. Nine, my time. Don't be late.
Mason drove Ethan to the airport, didn't try to stop him, and they set their first long-distance date for Saturday.
Breakfast first. Everything else can wait.
The diner by the rink, the booth under the broken neon. Two breakfast mugs. One check, split exactly down the middle.
I'm not ready for more. I don't know when I will be.
I'll ask again when it isn't a goodbye.
They had breakfast together before Ethan's flight; Ethan wasn't ready for more, and Mason said he'd ask again someday.
Take back the spare key.
I called their goalie coach last night. Just some notes on your glove side, so they don't —
I hold out my hand. He knows what for. The key comes off the ring slower than it went on.
Being needed isn't the same as being chosen.
He takes the nine o'clock flight. They both keep their jobs. Only one of them keeps the key.
Mason admitted calling Ethan's new goalie coach; Ethan took back the spare key and left without him.
No-Standing Zone

Mason stops trying to fix Ethan's life and tells him the plain truth instead. At the departures curb his hand stops halfway, and Ethan closes the rest of the distance himself. Their first long-distance date is Saturday, nine o'clock Ethan's time.
You can miss me without fixing my life.
Two Mugs, One Check

Ethan isn't ready to call it anything, and Mason doesn't make him. They split breakfast down the middle at the diner by the rink, then Ethan flies west to his own net. The question stays open, on purpose.
I'll ask again when it isn't a goodbye.
The Key Comes Off the Ring

Mason can't stop managing Ethan's career, even from two time zones away. Ethan takes back the spare key and gets on the plane alone. Both of them keep their jobs; only one of them learns the difference.
Being needed isn't the same as being chosen.
Seven Days, Two Cities
The first week after the trade, told twice: once from Ethan's new crease, once from the empty stall next to Mason's. It ends with one long-distance dinner, two time zones, and one shared calendar.
The two of them on the empty rink after practice, two jerseys and two numbers — your caption on the border.
Line Call: each shift, pick one of three agreed positions for Mason. A miss changes the post-game review, never anyone's skill.
A plain practice towel with Ethan's new number stitched on it — or a handwritten card, which counts exactly as much.
Off-day breakfast at the diner, or a long-distance dinner with both schedules on the table.
The post-practice rink photo, an empty airport seat, and a new-apartment video screenshot — taken only with consent.
A short voicemail before the move, and the first call across time zones — both of them promised in the same calendar.
Two city maps, two breakfast mugs, and the corrected interview draft in two handwritings.
Move the big explanation to before or after practice.
Change a scene's time or place — as long as both players could actually be there.
Add a third person (the physio, a linemate) with a clear reason to be in the room and only what they'd know.
No trade: the team swaps who starts instead, and they have to share the net.
They meet again after college, before either one has gone pro.
